# The LASSO

## Recall: Least Squares and Ridge Regression

Suppose we've selected a regression model:
$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots + \beta_pX_p + \epsilon,\qquad \epsilon \sim N(0,~\sigma^2)$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column .fragment .nonincremental}

**Least Squares:** Find $\beta$s that minimize
$$RSS=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\ \Big)^2$$

  + Goal of RSS: Make regression line "close to data"

:::

::: {.column .fragment .nonincremental}

**Ridge Regression:** Find $\beta$s that minimize
$$
\textrm{RSS} + \underbrace{\lambda\sum_{j = 1}^p \beta_j^2}_\text{Ridge Penalty} \qquad \textrm{where }  \lambda \geq 0
$$

  + Goal of Ridge Penalty: Make coefficients smaller

:::

::::

## LASSO Regression

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Least Squares: }& \text{Minimize RSS}\\
\text{Ridge Regression: }& \text{Minimize RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2
\end{aligned}$$

**Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator**: Find $\beta$s that minimize
$$
\textrm{RSS} + \underbrace{\lambda\sum_{j = 1}^p \big|\beta_j\big|}_\text{LASSO Penalty} \qquad \textrm{where }  \lambda \geq 0
$$

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

  + Goal of LASSO Penalty: Make coefficients smaller

  + Like Ridge, LASSO increases bias but decreases variance and (hopefully) MSE.

So how is LASSO different from Ridge?

:::

## Geometric Perspective: Two Types of Distance

How to measure distance between a point $x=(x_1, \dots, x_p)$ and the origin $(0, \dots, 0)$?


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**Euclidean distance:** "straight line" distance:
$$
\Vert x\Vert_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \dots + x_p^2} = \sqrt{ \sum_{j=1}^p x_j^2}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

  - Most common: Result of the Pythagorean theorem

  - Also called the **$\ell_2$ norm**

  - **Ridge** uses $\big(\Vert x\Vert_2\big)^2$ to "shrink" coefficients

:::

:::

::: {.column}

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**Manhattan distance:** "grid line" distance:
$$
\Vert x\Vert_1 = |x_1| + \dots + |x_p| = \sum_{j=1}^p |x_j|
$$

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

 - the **$\ell_1$ norm**

 - **LASSO** uses $\Vert x\Vert_1$ directly for shrinkage

:::

:::

## Consider: Different Distance, Different Emphasis

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Least Squares: }& \text{Minimize RSS}\\
\text{Ridge Regression: }& \text{Minimize RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2\\
\text{LASSO Regression: }& \text{Minimize RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \big|\beta_j\big|
\end{aligned}$$

::: {.nonincremental}

1. Suppose $\beta_j=\ -10$. Calculate $\beta_j^2$ and $\big|\beta_j\big|$, then explain why this shows that Ridge penalizes "big" coefficients more than LASSO.

2. Suppose $\beta_j=\ 0.1$. Calculate $\beta_j^2$ and $\big|\beta_j\big|$, then explain why this shows that LASSO penalizes "small" coefficients more than Ridge.

3. Hypothesize why LASSO might shrink coefficients to **exactly zero** more often than Ridge.

:::

## LASSO for Variable Selection

We've just uncovered why LASSO is a variable "**selection operator**":

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**Ridge *and* LASSO:** Coefficients with high variance are encouraged to shrink.

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**Ridge:** Penalty gets relatively smaller as coefficients get smaller

  + No benefit of making small coefficients zero.

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**LASSO:** Penalty gets relatively larger as coefficients get smaller

  + Bigger benefit of making small coefficients *precisely 0*.

  + $\beta_j=0$ $\implies$ $X_j$ removed from model!

  + This is variable selection!

:::

## Ridge vs. LASSO

::: {.nonincremental}

**Similarities:**

  - Fast to estimate models (similar to Least Squares)

  - Shrink coefficients: Increasing bias but reducing variance and MSE

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

**Differences:**

  - **LASSO performs variable selection simultaneously**, Ridge does not.

  - LASSO generally outperforms Ridge when some coefficients are *truly* zero.

  - Ridge generally outperforms LASSO when *all* coefficients are truly *non-zero*.

:::

# Case Study: Wine Acidity

## Wine Acidity

We study a "classic" dataset on red Vinho Verde wines grown in Northern Portugal.

::: {.nonincremental}

  + $n=200$ different wines

  + $Y$=Fixed Acidity

  + $X$=9 physical properties of the wine (e.g., residual sugar, pH, etc.) and average quality rating

:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.5
#| out-width: "80%"
wine <- read_delim("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/wine-quality/winequality-red.csv",
           delim = ";", escape_double = FALSE, trim_ws = TRUE)
wine <- wine[1:200,-8]
head(wine)
```

:::

## Wine Acidity: Response variable distribution

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(wine, aes(x = `fixed acidity`)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Y (Fixed Acidity)", 
       x = "Fixed Acidity") +
  theme_bw()
```


## Least Squares Estimates

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 0.5
#| out-width: "75%"
model_ls <- lm(`fixed acidity` ~ ., data = wine)
library(coefplot)
coefplot(model_ls, intercept = F, sort = "magnitude") +
  theme_bw() 
```

**Q:** Which coefficients will LASSO shrink to 0?

## LASSO in `R`

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1-9|8"
library(glmnet)
library(broom)
grid <- 10^(seq(-4, 1, length = 1000))
x <- model.matrix(`fixed acidity` ~ ., data = wine)[, -1]
y <- wine$`fixed acidity`
lasso_mod <- glmnet(x,
                    y, 
                    alpha = 1,
                    lambda = grid)
```


## LASSO Estimates (ggplot2)

Examine how LASSO coefficient estimates vary as $\lambda$ changes:

```{r}
tidied <- tidy(lasso_mod) %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)")
ggplot(tidied, aes(x = lambda, y = estimate, group = term, color = term)) +
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-4, -2, 0)),
                labels = c(".0001", ".01", "1")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  labs(title = "Coefficent estimates based on LASSO",
       x = expression(lambda ~ " (lambda)")) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 1))
```

## LASSO Estimates (base)

```{r}
plot(lasso_mod, sign.lambda = 1, label = TRUE)
```


## Cross-Validation for Optimal Tuning Parameter

To find the optimal tuning parameter, $\lambda$, we again use Cross-Validation

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "2-6|7-8|10-17"
#| output-location: column-fragment
set.seed(1010)
my_cv <- cv.glmnet(x,
                   y,
                   alpha = 1,
                   lambda = grid,
                   nfolds = 20)
best_L <- my_cv$lambda.min
reg_L <- my_cv$lambda.1se

tidied <- tidy(my_cv)
ggplot(tidied, aes(x = lambda, y = estimate)) + 
  geom_line(color = "red") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-4, -2, 0)),
                labels = c(".0001", ".01", "1")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
  labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Test MSE") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_L)
```

::: {.nonincremental .fragment}

+ Gray vertical line is optimal $\lambda$: Test MSE minimized at 0.4297.

+ (Ridge yields Test MSE of 0.4317)

:::

## Feature Selection

What features did the best $\lambda$ **select?**

```{r}
s <- which(lasso_mod$lambda==best_L)
names(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] != 0)[(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] != 0)]
```

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

What features did the best $\lambda$ **not** select?

```{r}
names(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] == 0)[(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] == 0)]
```

**Why not Quality, Free Sulfur Dioxide, Residual Sugar, and Total Sulfur Dioxide?**

:::

## Back to the Least Squares Estimates

```{r}
#| output-location: column
model_ls <- lm(`fixed acidity`~.,data=wine)
library(coefplot)
coefplot(model_ls, intercept = F, sort = "magnitude") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Coefficient Plot")
```


## Back to the Least Squares Estimates

```{r}
#| output-location: column
model_ls <- lm(`fixed acidity`~.,data=wine)
library(coefplot)
coefplot(model_ls, intercept = F, sort = "magnitude") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-.12, .18)) +
  labs(title = "Coefficient Plot (Zoomed In)")
```

LASSO removed only a *high variance* coefficient that was near 0.
